title: Linear & binary search
examples: When should I use binary search instead of linear search?
What must I do with the list before I can use binary search?
Can binary search work if the list is not sorted?

explain.say: Today we are learning about two ways to find things in a list.
Linear search checks every item one by one in order.

items: Check if it is the target
If no, move to next item

explain.say: Binary search only works if the list is already sorted first.
The first step of binary search is finding the middle element.
Next, we compare the target value to the middle element found.
If the target is not the middle, we cut the list in half.

faq.q: Do I have to sort the list before I can use binary search?
faq.a: Yes, the list absolutely must be sorted in ascending order for binary search to work correctly. If it is not sorted, the algorithm will likely fail to find the correct item.
asks: Does the order matter for binary search?
Can I skip the sorting step?

faq.q: How many steps does binary search take compared to linear search?
faq.a: Binary search is much faster for large lists because it eliminates half the data in every step. Linear search checks every single item one after the other.
asks: What is the time complexity difference?

faq.q: What if the item I am looking for is not in the list?
faq.a: Both searches will eventually tell you that the item was not found. In binary search, the process will end when the search space becomes empty.
asks: How do I know if it's missing?

faq.q: Can I use binary search on things that are not numbers?
faq.a: Yes, as long as the items can be put into a definite order, like alphabetical order for words. The concept of 'sorted' applies to many data types.

faq.q: Is there a specific formula for finding the middle point?
faq.a: The middle index is usually found by adding the start and end indices and dividing by two. This keeps the search balanced.
asks: How do I calculate the middle?
What is the formula for the midpoint?

facts: Linear search checks elements sequentially, one after the other.
Binary search requires the data set to be sorted first.
Binary search repeatedly divides the search interval in half.
For a list of size N, linear search takes up to N steps.

quiz.say: A list is: [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]. We search for 20.

options.show: The search checks the middle element (30) first.
options.say: The search checks the middle element (30) first.

quiz.why: The middle element, 30, is checked first because the list is sorted, which is the core idea of binary search.

wrong.0: This is guessing; binary search uses the sorted order to eliminate half the list.
wrong.1: The target might be 20, which is not 30, so you must continue comparing.
wrong.3: This is linear search, which ignores the efficiency of binary search.

quiz.say: If a list is [5, 15, 25, 35, 45] and we search for 15.

options.show: Since 15 is less than 25, the search continues in the left half [5, 15].
options.say: Since 15 is less than 25, the search continues in the left half [5, 15].

quiz.why: Because 15 is smaller than the middle element 25, we know the target must be in the left portion of the list.

wrong.1: We should not jump to the next element; we must use the comparison to narrow the search area.
wrong.2: Binary search's strength is that it never needs to restart from the beginning.
wrong.3: We must always check if the target matches the current middle element before discarding half the list.

quiz.say: What is the most important precondition for binary search?

options.show: The data set must be sorted in ascending or descending order.
options.say: The data set must be sorted in ascending or descending order.

options.show: The list must have an even number of items.
options.say: The list must have an even number of items.

options.show: The list must contain only numbers.
options.say: The list must contain only numbers.

options.show: The search must start from the first item.
options.say: The search must start from the first item.

quiz.why: Sorting allows the algorithm to confidently discard half the remaining data in each step.

wrong.1: The list can have any number of items, even or odd.
wrong.2: It can work with words or other ordered data types.
wrong.3: While it starts conceptually, the first action is finding the middle, not checking the first item.
